# Conduit

> Broker-neutral data streaming engine and Kafka Connect replacement. Pipelines move records from
> source connectors to destination connectors with processors in between; any-language plugins
> over gRPC/WASM; embeddable; agent-legible with stable error codes and an MCP server.

## 1. Pipeline configuration schema

### Versions
- 2.0
- 2.1
- 2.2 (latest)

| Pipelines | `pipelines` | `[]Pipeline` | yes |

| WindowNackThreshold | `window-nack-threshold` | `*int` | no |

### Legacy v1 (1.1)

v1 pipeline configs key `pipelines`, `connectors`, and `processors` by map (`pipelines: {<id>: {...}}`) instead of v2's ordered list, so processor and connector ordering within a v1 file is not deterministic. v1 has no `plugin`/`condition` processor fields and no top-level `dead-letter-queue` before 1.1. New pipelines should use v2.

## 2. Built-in connectors (6)

### file (v0.10.8)

A file source and destination plugin for Conduit.

**How it works**

The Source connector listens for changes appended to the source file and
sends records with the changes.
The Destination connector receives records and writes them to a file.

**Source**

The Source connector only cares to have a valid path, even if the file
doesn't exist, it will still run and wait until a file with the configured
name is there, then it will start listening to changes and sending records.

**Destination**

The Destination connector will create the file if it doesn't exist, and
records with changes will be appended to the destination file when received.

Author: Meroxa, Inc.

#### Source parameters

| Key | Type | Default | Required | Description | Validations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string |  | yes | Path is the file path used by the connector to read/write records. | required |
| `sdk.batch.delay` | duration | 0 | no | Maximum delay before an incomplete batch is read from the source. |  |
| `sdk.batch.size` | int | 0 | no | Maximum size of batch before it gets read from the source. | greater-than(-1) |
| `sdk.schema.context.enabled` | bool | true | no | Specifies whether to use a schema context name. If set to false, no schema context name will be used, and schemas will be saved with the subject name specified in the connector (not safe because of name conflicts). |  |
| `sdk.schema.context.name` | string |  | no | Schema context name to be used. Used as a prefix for all schema subject names. If empty, defaults to the connector ID. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.key.enabled` | bool | false | no | Whether to extract and encode the record key with a schema. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.key.subject` | string | key | no | The subject of the key schema. If the record metadata contains the field "opencdc.collection" it is prepended to the subject name and separated with a dot. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.payload.enabled` | bool | false | no | Whether to extract and encode the record payload with a schema. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.payload.subject` | string | payload | no | The subject of the payload schema. If the record metadata contains the field "opencdc.collection" it is prepended to the subject name and separated with a dot. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.type` | string | avro | no | The type of the payload schema. | inclusion(avro) |

| `path` | string |  | yes | Path is the file path used by the connector to read/write records. | required |
| `sdk.batch.delay` | duration | 0 | no | Maximum delay before an incomplete batch is written to the destination. |  |

Note that if `sdk.batch.size` is bigger than `sdk.rate.burst`, the effective batch size will be equal to `sdk.rate.burst`. | greater-than(-1) |

### generator (v0.10.4)

A plugin capable of generating dummy records (in different formats).

The generator is capable of generating dummy records (in JSON format). The
connector makes it possible to configure the records' fields, the operation
(whether the record was created, updated or deleted), the rate at which records
are produced, and other properties of the connector.

**Examples**

**Bursts**

The following configuration generates 100 records in bursts of 10 records each,
with a 1-second sleep time between bursts.

> [!NOTE]
> The generator currently has no concept of resuming work. For instance, below
> we have configured it to generate 100 records, but if we restart the pipeline
> (by stopping and starting the pipeline or by restarting Conduit), then it will
> start generating the 100 records from scratch.

```yaml
version: 2.2
pipelines:
  - id: example
    status: running
    connectors:
      - id: example
        type: source
        plugin: generator
        settings:
          # global settings
          rate: 10
          recordCount: 100
          burst.generateTime: 1s
          burst.sleepTime: 1s
          # default collection
          format.type: structured
          format.options.id: int
          format.options.name: string
          operations: create
```

**Collections**

The following configuration generates records forever with a steady rate of 1000
records per second. Records are generated in the `users` and `orders` collections.
The generated records have a different format, depending on the collection they
belong to.

```yaml
version: 2.2
pipelines:
  - id: example
    status: running
    connectors:
      - id: example
        type: source
        plugin: generator
        settings:
          # global settings
          rate: 1000
          # collection "users"
          collections.users.format.type: structured
          collections.users.format.options.id: int
          collections.users.format.options.name: string
          collections.users.operations: create
          # collection "orders"
          collections.orders.format.type: raw
          collections.orders.format.options.id: int
          collections.orders.format.options.product: string
          collections.orders.operations: create,update,delete
```


Author: Meroxa, Inc.

### kafka (v0.12.6)

A Kafka source and destination plugin for Conduit, written in Go.

**Source**

A Kafka source connector is represented by a single consumer in a Kafka consumer
group. By virtue of that, a source's logical position is the respective
consumer's offset in Kafka. Internally, though, we're not saving the offset as
the position: instead, we're saving the consumer group ID, since that's all
which is needed for Kafka to find the offsets for our consumer.

A source is getting associated with a consumer group ID the first time the
`Read()` method is called.

**Destination**

The destination connector writes records to Kafka.

**Output format**

The output format can be adjusted using configuration options provided by the
connector SDK:

- `sdk.record.format`: used to choose the format
- `sdk.record.format.options`: used to configure the specifics of the chosen format

See [this article](https://conduitdata.io/docs/using/connectors/configuration-parameters/output-format) for more
info on configuring the output format.

**Batching**

Batching can also be configured using connector SDK provided options:

- `sdk.batch.size`: maximum number of records in batch before it gets written to
  the destination (defaults to 0, no batching)
- `sdk.batch.delay`: maximum delay before an incomplete batch is written to the
  destination (defaults to 0, no limit)

Author: Meroxa, Inc.

### log (v0.7.5)

A destination connector that logs all incoming records.

**Destination**

The destination connector logs records using the built-in Conduit logger.

Example log message:

```
{"level":"info","record":{"position":"cjI=","operation":"create","metadata":{"foo":"bar","opencdc.version":"v1"},"key":{"my-id-field":1},"payload":{"before":nil,"after":{"my-payload-field":false}}}}
```

Note that the `position` field is base64 encoded, same goes for a key or payload
that contains raw byte data.

Keep in mind that Conduit's log level needs to be configured lower or equal to
the log level of the connector in order for the records to show up in the logs.

**Known issues**

- **Only when using as a [standalone connector](https://conduitdata.io/docs/core-concepts#standalone-connector)**: Messages larger than 64KB will not be logged when using `log.level` as `info`.
  This is a known issue caused by the default buffer value of `go-plugin`. More information can be found in [this comment](https://github.com/ConduitIO/conduit-connector-log/issues/81#issuecomment-2904224580).


Author: Meroxa, Inc.

| `message` | string |  | no | Optional message that should be added to the log output of every record. |  |
| `sdk.batch.delay` | duration | 0 | no | Maximum delay before an incomplete batch is written to the destination. |  |

### postgres (v0.14.4)

Conduit connector for PostgreSQL

**Source**

The Postgres Source Connector connects to a database with the provided `url` and
starts creating records for each change detected in the provided tables.

Upon starting, the source takes a snapshot of the provided tables in the database,
then switches into CDC mode. In CDC mode, the plugin reads from a buffer of CDC events.

**Snapshot**

When the connector first starts, snapshot mode is enabled. The connector acquires
a read-only lock on the tables, and then reads all rows of the tables into Conduit.
Once all rows in that initial snapshot are read the connector releases its lock and
switches into CDC mode.

This behavior is enabled by default, but can be turned off by adding
`"snapshotMode": "never"` to the Source configuration.

**Change Data Capture**

This connector implements Change Data Capture (CDC) features for PostgreSQL by
creating a logical replication slot and a publication that listens to changes in the
configured tables. Every detected change is converted into a record. If there are no
records available, the connector blocks until a record is available or the connector
receives a stop signal.

**Logical Replication Configuration**

When the connector switches to CDC mode, it attempts to run the initial setup commands
to create its logical replication slot and publication. It will connect to an existing
slot if one with the configured name exists.

The Postgres user specified in the connection URL must have sufficient privileges to
run all of these setup commands, or it will fail.

Example pipeline configuration that's using logical replication:

```yaml
version: 2.2
pipelines:
  - id: pg-to-log
    status: running
    connectors:
      - id: pg
        type: source
        plugin: builtin:postgres
        settings:
          url: "postgres://exampleuser:examplepass@localhost:5433/exampledb?sslmode=disable"
          tables: "users"
          cdcMode: "logrepl"
          logrepl.publicationName: "examplepub"
          logrepl.slotName: "exampleslot"
      - id: log
        type: destination
        plugin: builtin:log
        settings:
          level: info
```

:warning: When the connector or pipeline is deleted, the connector will automatically
attempt to delete the replication slot and publication. This is the default behaviour
and can be disabled by setting `logrepl.autoCleanup` to `false`.

**Key Handling**

The connector will automatically look up the primary key column for the specified tables
and use them as the key value. If that can't be determined, the connector will return
an error.

The table's `REPLICA IDENTITY` must carry the primary key in deletes. `DEFAULT` and
`FULL` always do. `USING INDEX` does only if the index includes the primary-key
column; otherwise Postgres sends deletes without the key, and they cannot be applied
downstream. The source refuses to open on such a table with the error code
`postgres.replica_identity.excludes_key`. Fix it with
`ALTER TABLE <table> REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, or use a unique index that includes the
primary key.

**Numeric Columns**

A `numeric` column with a precision and scale, `numeric(p,s)`, is an Avro
`decimal(p,s)` and its values are `big.Rat`.

A `numeric` column **without** a precision and scale can hold any value Postgres
can store, which no Avro `decimal` can. With `logrepl.withAvroSchema: true` (the
default) it is an Avro `string` holding the exact text of the value, with its
scale (`1.50` stays `1.50`), and `NaN`, `Infinity` and
`-Infinity` as those three words: **a consumer of such a column must handle
them**, a plain decimal parser will reject them. Earlier versions used `decimal(65535, 65531)`, which could not encode a
value of 10000 or more and stopped the pipeline. The first record after an
upgrade registers a new schema version for the table; consumers must read the
field as a string. This connector's destination writes the string to a `numeric`
column exactly.

**Known issue:** a zero with a display scale reads as `0` in the snapshot and as
`0.000` (its stored text) in change data capture. The values are numerically
equal; only the text differs. Tracked in
[#391](https://github.com/ConduitIO/conduit-connector-postgres/issues/391).

So the Go type of an unconstrained `numeric` depends on the setting: a `string`
with `logrepl.withAvroSchema: true`, a `big.Rat` with `false`.

Without an Avro schema, a `numeric` is a `big.Rat`; `NaN`, `Infinity` and
`-Infinity` are the strings `"NaN"`, `"Infinity"` and `"-Infinity"`, and the same
applies to the elements of `numeric[]` (finite elements are unchanged). A `NULL`
stays `NULL`.

`NaN` in a `numeric(p,s)` column (the infinities cannot be stored there) cannot
be an Avro decimal, and the connector never replaces it with `NULL` or a number:
the source stops with the error code `postgres.source.numeric_not_representable`,
which names the table, the column, the value and the row's key. To continue:

- **Change data capture:** restart once with `logrepl.withAvroSchema: false`
  from the same position. The value is delivered as a string. **Then set it
  back to `true` as soon as that record has been delivered.** Without an Avro
  schema a finite `numeric` is a `big.Rat`, which a standalone connector
  cannot send to Conduit (#378): the next finite numeric would stop the
  pipeline. Built-in pipelines are not affected.
  On a standalone connector the SDK also fails the whole read batch on the
  first record it cannot send, so if the NaN/Infinity record or its batch
  contains any finite numeric, it is never delivered with Avro off and this
  workaround does not help (#378 is the fix). While Avro is off,
  JSON-serializing destinations receive a finite numeric as the string `"3/2"`.
- **Snapshot:** `UPDATE` the row to a finite value (or `NULL`) and restart.
- Removing the row, or adding a `CHECK` constraint, does not help for a change
  that is already in the WAL: it is read again after every restart. Do not drop
  the replication slot to get past it, that loses the position. A constraint
  only keeps new bad values out.

**Infinite Dates and Timestamps**

`date`, `timestamp` and `timestamptz` columns can hold `infinity` and
`-infinity`. The Avro date and timestamp types cannot represent them. Earlier
versions wrote them as `1970-01-02` and `1969-12-31` (dates) without any error.

- With `logrepl.withAvroSchema: true` (the default), the source stops with the
  error code `postgres.source.temporal_not_representable`, which names the
  table, the column and the value. Removing the row does not help once the
  change is in the WAL: set `logrepl.withAvroSchema` to `false`.
- With `logrepl.withAvroSchema: false`, the values are emitted as the strings
  `"infinity"` and `"-infinity"`.

The same applies per element of `date[]`, `timestamp[]`, `timestamptz[]` and
`numeric[]` (for `numeric[]`, `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` elements are
emitted as strings; finite elements are unchanged). The connector has no Avro
mapping for array columns, so with the default `logrepl.withAvroSchema: true`
a table with an array column already stops with a schema error before any
record is emitted.

**Before Image of Updates and Deletes**

`Payload.Before` is set only when Postgres sends the whole old row, which it does
under `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`. Under `DEFAULT` and `USING INDEX`, Postgres sends only
the identity columns of the old row, so deletes and key-changing updates carry no
`Before`. The deleted row's key is in the record `Key`. A key-changing update carries
the new key in `Key`; the old key is not carried. If you need the old row or the old
key, set `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` on the table.

:warning: The Postgres destination does not delete the old row when a primary key
changes. It upserts on the new key, so a primary-key-changing `UPDATE` leaves the row
under its old key in the destination next to the new one. This happens with or without
Avro and under `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` as well. It is a known destination bug
([#386](https://github.com/ConduitIO/conduit-connector-postgres/issues/386)). Until it
is fixed, avoid changing primary keys on tables replicated to Postgres, or reconcile
the old rows by hand.

**Delete With a Missing Key**

**Symptom.** The pipeline fails and keeps failing after restarts with
`postgres.replica_identity.excludes_key: delete on table "<table>" (WAL LSN <a>, in the
transaction that commits at LSN <b>) arrived without a value for key column ...`.
The replication slot retains WAL while it is stuck.

**Diagnosis.** The table's `REPLICA IDENTITY` was changed while the pipeline was
running, to `USING INDEX` on an index whose key columns do not include the primary key
(columns in `INCLUDE` do not count), or the identity index was dropped. Postgres then
sends the delete without the key. Check with
`SELECT relreplident FROM pg_class WHERE oid = '<table>'::regclass` (`i` is
`USING INDEX`).

**Remediation.**

1. Fix the identity so that new deletes carry the key:
   `ALTER TABLE <table> REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, or `REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT`, or
   `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX <index>` on a unique index that has the primary key
   among its key columns. This does not repair the change already in the WAL. A restart
   alone fails on it again.
2. Stop the pipeline. Postgres refuses to read or advance a slot while a connection
   uses it.
3. Find the row. The error carries no row values, because they would end up in logs.
   Read the stuck transaction from the slot instead, as a superuser or a role with
   `REPLICATION`. Peeking does not consume anything. `<c>` is the commit LSN `<b>`
   from the error with its low hex part incremented by one (`0/40C5318` becomes
   `0/40C5319`); the error prints it:

   ```sql
   SELECT xid, lsn, encode(data, 'escape') AS message
   FROM pg_logical_slot_peek_binary_changes(
          '<slot name>', '<c>', NULL,
          'proto_version', '1', 'publication_names', '<publication name>');
   ```

   Use the values of `logrepl.slotName` and `logrepl.publicationName` (defaults
   `conduitslot` and `conduitpub`).
   The output can start with earlier transactions that the pipeline already delivered
   but Postgres has not yet been told about (the connector reports its position
   periodically). They can contain the same value as the stuck delete, so do not read
   them. Read only the transaction (`xid`) that contains the `D` row whose `lsn` is the
   WAL LSN `<a>` in the error.
   Each row is one pgoutput message. `B` and `C` begin and commit the transaction. `R`
   names a table and its columns. `I`, `U` and `D` are the changes. A `K` tuple follows
   the table's object id: a 2-byte column count, then one entry per column, `n` for NULL
   or `t`, a 4-byte length and the text value. For this error the only non-null columns
   are those of the identity index, so the readable text is the value to look for, for
   example `222` in a `D` row that shows `K ... n t ... 222 n`. Postgres only accepts a
   unique index as a replica identity, so that value identifies the row in the
   destination. Only tables in the publication appear, which are the tables the pipeline
   captures.
4. Delete that row from the destination yourself. The change has no key, so the pipeline
   cannot do it. Then work out what else step 5 would skip. It skips every change the
   peek lists before the stuck one, and the other changes of the stuck transaction.
   Postgres has not been told they are done, and the pipeline may have read them
   without the destination writing them before it stopped. Get the source connector's
   last acknowledged position from Conduit:
   `GET /v1/connectors/<source connector id>`, field `sourceState.position`. It is
   base64 of JSON, for example
   `{"version":2,"type":2,"last_lsn":"0/40845E8","tx_commit_lsn":"0/40846E8","tx_seq":1}`
   (decode it with `base64 -d`). Conduit sets it only when the destination acknowledges a
   record, never when the source reads one, so `last_lsn` is the WAL LSN of the last
   change the destination has confirmed. If Conduit was restarted since the pipeline
   stopped, it reports the last position it saved, which can be slightly older; that errs
   on the safe side. Find the peek row of kind `I`, `U` or `D` whose `lsn` equals
   `last_lsn`. Ignore `B` and `C` rows: a `C` row can show the same number as the first
   change after it. If several rows share that `lsn` (a `COPY` or another statement
   that changes many rows can do that), use `tx_seq`. It numbers the transaction's
   `I`, `U`, `D` and `T` (truncate) rows in the order listed, starting at 1 after its
   `B` row. `R` (relation), `Y` (type) and `O` (origin) rows are not counted. The row
   with that number is the one to match, and it is an `I`, `U` or `D` row. The matched row
   itself and everything listed before it are in the destination. For each change
   listed after it, up to the stuck one and including the rest of the stuck transaction,
   check the destination for its rows and apply any that are missing by hand (`I` and
   `U` carry the full new row; `D` carries the identity columns). If no row matches,
   treat every listed change as unconfirmed. A position without `last_lsn` (a pipeline
   still in its snapshot) matches nothing.
5. Skip the transaction. Use the same `<c>` as in step 3. Writing it as a literal is
   deliberate: `'<b>'::pg_lsn + 1` only works from Postgres 14.
   - Postgres 11 or later:
     `SELECT pg_replication_slot_advance('<slot name>', '<c>');`
   - Postgres 10 has no such function. Consume the changes up to `<c>` instead. This
     skips exactly the same changes and needs no new snapshot:
     `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_logical_slot_get_binary_changes('<slot name>', '<c>', NULL, 'proto_version', '1', 'publication_names', '<publication name>');`

   Advancing to `<c>` is what skips the transaction. Advancing to the change LSN
   (`<a>`) or to the commit LSN `<b>` itself does not: Postgres replays the transaction
   and the pipeline fails on the same delete.
6. Start the pipeline.

**Skipping the transaction skips that change, and it skips the whole transaction,
including its other changes to captured tables.** Skipping data is your decision and the
connector cannot check it for you.

**Unchanged TOASTed Columns**

Postgres stores large field values (`text`, `bytea`, `jsonb`, and other
variable-length types past a size threshold) out-of-line using
[TOAST](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-toast.html). When a row is
updated but a TOASTed column is **not** changed, Postgres omits that column's value
from the logical-replication message to avoid re-transmitting large unchanged data.

For such columns, this connector **omits the field from the record payload** rather
than emitting it as `NULL`. Emitting `NULL` would be silent data corruption — a
downstream sink cannot distinguish "the value was set to NULL" from "the value did
not change". Omission preserves that distinction: absence means "unchanged".

What this means for your destination:

- **Partial-update / upsert sinks** (including this connector's own Postgres
  destination, which builds its `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET` clause only from the
  fields present in the payload) handle omission correctly — an absent field is left
  untouched in the target row.
- **Full-row / full-document replace sinks** must treat an absent field as
  "unchanged" and preserve the existing target value. If a sink cannot do this, set
  `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` on the source table. Under `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` the old
  row image carries every column, and this connector backfills unchanged TOASTed
  values from it so the payload is always complete.

With the default `logrepl.withAvroSchema: true` and the default
`REPLICA IDENTITY`, an update that leaves a TOASTed column unchanged still stops the
source: the field is omitted, but the Avro payload schema requires it, so the record
cannot be encoded
([#383](https://github.com/ConduitIO/conduit-connector-postgres/issues/383)). Set
`REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` on such tables.

**Limitations**

- **`TRUNCATE` is not propagated.** OpenCDC has no truncate operation, so a
  `TRUNCATE` on a published table produces no record: rows it removed remain in
  the destination. If the publication publishes `truncate` (the one the
  connector creates does by default), the connector logs a `WARN` ("TRUNCATE was NOT
  propagated") naming the table and the LSN, at most once a minute per table.
  A restricted or user-supplied publication (for example
  `publish = 'insert, update, delete'`) never sends the message, so there is
  no warning and no other signal. The `suppressed` field counts the TRUNCATEs
  of that table the rate limit swallowed since the previous warning; when
  another table's warning evicts an expired entry that still holds a count, a
  one-line summary with that count is logged. Treat the log lines as a signal,
  not a precise counter: a count still pending when the process exits is
  lost. Inserts, updates and deletes around the `TRUNCATE` are delivered as
  usual. A configurable policy for TRUNCATE is planned. Until then, treat the
  warning as a signal to reconcile the destination by hand.

**Destination**

The Postgres Destination takes a Conduit record and stores it using a SQL statement.
The Destination is designed to handle different payloads and keys. Because of this,
each record is individually parsed and upserted.

**Handling record operations**

Based on the `Operation` field in the record, the destination will either insert,
update or delete the record in the target table. Snapshot records are always inserted.

If the target table already contains a record with the same key as a record being
inserted, the record will be updated (upserted). This can overwrite and thus potentially
lose data, so keys should be assigned correctly from the Source.

If the target table does not contain a record with the same key as a record being
deleted, the record will be ignored.

If there is no key, the record will be simply appended.

**Numeric columns**

Decimal values (`big.Rat`) are sent to Postgres as exact decimal strings, and
Postgres applies the column's precision and scale itself when it stores the
value. The destination never reads or caches a column's scale, so an
`ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE numeric(p,s)` takes effect on the next
write without restarting the pipeline, and the table is resolved through the
connection's `search_path` like the rest of the statement.

Postgres rounds half away from zero when a value has more fractional digits
than the column's scale, and rejects a value that exceeds the column's
precision (`numeric field overflow`). A rejected batch is not acknowledged.

A decimal that has no finite expansion, such as 1/3, is truncated toward zero
after 1001 fractional digits before it is sent. So is a decimal that terminates
but needs more than 16383 fractional digits, which Postgres rejects on every
numeric column. Postgres allows a column scale of at most 1000, so the
truncation never changes the result of the column's rounding. An unconstrained
`numeric` column stores all 1001 digits.

The destination no longer checks that the target column is numeric. The general
rule: any column whose text input accepts the decimal string stores it.
Postgres converts the string, and the examples below were checked on
Postgres 17.5:

- `integer`, `smallint`, `bigint`: stored if the value is whole. A fractional
  value is rejected, except on a destination that was already running when the
  column was changed to an integer type: the cached prepared statement still
  types the parameter as `numeric`, so 5/2 is silently rounded to 3
  (see #367).
- `real`, `float8`: stored as the nearest binary float.
- `money`: rounded to the locale's fraction digits (1/3 is stored as `$0.33`).
- `oid`: stored if the value is a whole number (7 is stored as `7`).
- `text`: stored as the decimal string. `varchar(n)` and `char(n)`: rejected
  with 22001 if the string is longer than `n`.
- `boolean`: 1 is stored as `true` and 0 as `false`; other values are rejected.
- `date`: 20261012 is stored as `2026-10-12`.
- `timestamp`: 20261012 is stored as `2026-10-12 00:00:00`.
- `timestamptz`: 20261012 is stored as `2026-10-12 00:00:00+00` (session time
  zone UTC).
- `interval`: 12345 is stored as `03:25:45`.
- `json`, `jsonb`: 1/4 is stored as the JSON number `0.25`.
- `bytea`: 5/2 is stored as `\x322e35`, the ASCII bytes of `2.5`.
- `bit(n)`: stored if the decimal string is exactly `n` binary digits (101 is
  stored as `101` in a `bit(3)`).
- `time`, `inet`: rejected.

Every accepted conversion to a non-numeric type is a silent coercion if the
schema maps a numeric field to the wrong column, so check the mapping.


Author: Meroxa, Inc.

### s3 (v0.9.5)

An S3 source and destination plugin for Conduit, written in Go.

The S3 connector is one of [Conduit](https://github.com/ConduitIO/conduit)
builtin plugins. It provides both, a source and a destination S3 connectors.

**Source**

The S3 Source Connector connects to a S3 bucket with the provided
configurations, using `aws.bucket`, `aws.accessKeyId`,`aws.secretAccessKey` and
`aws.region`. If the bucket doesn't exist, or the permissions fail, then an
error will occur. After that, the `Open` method is called to start the
connection from the provided position.

**Change Data Capture (CDC)**

This connector implements CDC features for S3 by scanning the bucket for changes
every `pollingPeriod` and detecting any change that happened after a certain
timestamp. These changes (update, delete, create) are then inserted into a
buffer that is checked on each Read request.

* To capture "delete" and "update", the S3 bucket versioning must be enabled.
* To capture "create" actions, the bucket versioning doesn't matter.

**Position Handling**

The connector goes through two modes.

* Snapshot mode: which loops through the S3 bucket and returns the objects that
  are already in there. The _Position_ during this mode is the object key
  attached to an underscore, an "s" for snapshot, and the _maxLastModifiedDate_
  found so far. As an example: "thisIsAKey_s12345", which makes the connector
  know at what mode it is and what object it last read. The
  _maxLastModifiedDate_ will be used when changing to CDC mode, the iterator
  will capture changes that happened after that.

* CDC mode: this mode iterates through the S3 bucket every `pollingPeriod` and
  captures new actions made on the bucket. the _Position_ during this mode is
  the object key attached to an underscore, a "c" for CDC, and the object's
  _lastModifiedDate_ in seconds. As an example: "thisIsAKey_c1634049397". This
  position is used to resume from the last record returned.

  **CDC mode is listing based and best effort, bounded by `lookbackPeriod`.**
  It detects changes by listing the bucket, which cannot be lossless: an
  object that becomes visible in a listing late can be missed. Lossless S3
  change capture needs bucket event notifications, which this connector does
  not use. Every poll selects the objects modified since `lookbackPeriod`
  (default 5m) before the newest object seen so far, and skips versions it
  already delivered, so objects that become visible late, within that
  window, are picked up: S3 stamps an object with the time its upload began,
  a multipart upload with the time it was initiated, and lists in key order.
  The object store's own timestamps decide, so the clock of the machine
  running Conduit does not matter, with one exception: the newest timestamp
  is capped at this machine's clock, so one bogus timestamp from the future
  (a store clock that stepped forward, or a misbehaving endpoint) cannot hide
  the objects written after it. The cap lowers the window's start, which
  causes redelivery. If this machine's clock is behind the store's by more
  than `lookbackPeriod` the source logs a warning with the code
  `s3.source.host_clock_behind_store`: the window is stretched by the skew.

  Delivery is at-least-once. After a restart the objects modified within
  `lookbackPeriod` of the newest object are delivered again. The snapshot
  hands over to CDC from the newest object that existed when the snapshot
  started (found by one extra listing of the prefix, one request per 1000
  keys, at the start of the snapshot), minus `lookbackPeriod`, so CDC
  redelivers the objects written while the snapshot ran, however long it
  took, plus those within `lookbackPeriod` before it started. On a bucket
  that was bulk loaded recently this can be every object of the load.

  The versions remembered for deduplication are limited to about 256 MiB
  (peak memory of a poll is about 1.5 times that, candidates included). If
  the objects inside the window need more, the window is **shortened**
  instead of stopping the source: the oldest remembered entries are
  forgotten by whole seconds and the window starts just above them. The
  source logs a warning with the code `s3.source.dedupe_window_shrunk`
  naming the effective lookback and the number of forgotten entries. While
  the window is shortened, an object that becomes visible late by more than
  the effective lookback can be missed, so the tolerance for late-visible
  objects is lower than `lookbackPeriod`; lower `lookbackPeriod` to avoid
  the shrinking. The source stops, with the error
  `s3.source.dedupe_window_overflow` (after a warning), only if the versions
  sharing a single second of `LastModified` do not fit, or when entries
  stamped at or after this machine's present second (a store clock that is
  ahead, or bogus timestamps from the future) take the budget: a shortened
  window never starts later than the present second, because that would hide
  the objects written from now on, so the source stops instead (the message
  names the clock skew and says to fix the clock). A store clock that is ahead
  by less than `lookbackPeriod` is normal and does not stop the source as long
  as the entries stamped in the present and the future fit the budget. A
  future-stamped object can therefore raise the start of the window at most
  up to the present second, never past it. The shortened window is not
  remembered across restarts: after a restart the window is rebuilt from the
  position and shortened again, so a restart delivers the window's objects
  again (duplicates, never a skip). When more objects share a second than
  one poll can hand over, they are delivered over several polls, oldest
  first, and the newest tracked entries may be dropped from tracking to make
  room; those are delivered again later (duplicates). A catch-up after
  downtime is delivered in bounded batches, oldest first. A resume position
  with a timestamp in the future, which only an older release could have
  written, is clamped to this machine's clock with a warning.

  Known limits (listing cannot see these, or sees them too late):
  * an upload that takes longer than `lookbackPeriod` to complete is missed
    when newer objects were seen in the meantime (multipart uploads carry
    their initiation time);
  * replica buckets whose replication lag exceeds `lookbackPeriod`;
  * an identical re-put of an object within the same second is not seen as a
    change;
  * in an unversioned bucket an overwrite is reported as a create (there is
    no older version to compare with) and a delete is not reported;
  * in a versioned bucket intermediate versions that appear and are
    superseded within one poll are not emitted, only the latest; removing a
    delete marker (undelete) and permanently deleting the latest version are
    not emitted;
  * a GetObject that fails for another reason than the object having been
    deleted, for example an object archived to Glacier or Deep Archive,
    stops the source with that error.

  Objects deleted between being listed and being read are skipped, in the
  snapshot and in CDC. Values of `lookbackPeriod` above 1h log a warning and
  above 24h are rejected.

**Record Keys**

The S3 object key uniquely identifies the objects in an Amazon S3 bucket, which
is why a record key is the key read from the S3 bucket.

**Destination**

The S3 Destination Connector connects to an S3 bucket with the provided
configurations, using `aws.bucket`, `aws.accessKeyId`,`aws.secretAccessKey` and
`aws.region`. If the permissions fail, the connector will not be ready for
writing to S3.

**Writer**

The S3 destination writer has a buffer with the size of `bufferSize`, for each
time `Write` is called, a new record is added to the buffer. When the buffer is
full, all the records from it will be written to the S3 bucket, and an ack
function will be called for each record after being written.

Author: Meroxa, Inc.

#### Source parameters

| Key | Type | Default | Required | Description | Validations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aws.accessKeyId` | string |  | yes | AWS access key id. | required |
| `aws.bucket` | string |  | yes | the AWS S3 bucket name. | required |
| `aws.endpoint` | string |  | no | The endpoint to connect to. Set this when using an S3-compatible object store such as MinIO (for example http://localhost:9000). Leave empty to use the default AWS endpoints. The AWS_ENDPOINT_URL environment variable is also honored when this is empty. Note that an http:// endpoint sends every request, including the SigV4 Authorization header that carries the access key ID, in the clear: use https:// for anything that is not on localhost. |  |
| `aws.pathStyle` | bool | false | no | Use path-style addressing (http://endpoint/bucket/key) instead of virtual-hosted addressing (http://bucket.endpoint/key). Set this to true when using an S3-compatible store that does not support virtual-hosted addressing. The default MinIO setup (started without MINIO_DOMAIN) is one: it ignores the bucket in the host name and takes the first path segment as the bucket instead. What comes back depends on the key: with a prefix configured the remaining segments are still a key, so PutObject fails with a 404 NoSuchBucket; without a prefix there is no key left and MinIO answers with a 400 MalformedXML. Leave false for AWS S3. |  |
| `aws.region` | string |  | yes | the AWS S3 bucket region | required |
| `aws.secretAccessKey` | string |  | yes | AWS secret access key. | required |
| `lookbackPeriod` | duration | 5m | no | How far back, from the newest object seen, every CDC poll looks for objects that became visible late. S3 stamps an object with the time its upload began (a multipart upload with the time it was initiated), not the time it completed, and lists in key order, so an object can show up after newer ones were already delivered. Each poll selects the objects modified since (newest LastModified seen - lookbackPeriod) that were not delivered yet. Listing based CDC is best effort and bounded by this value: an upload that completes later than this value after newer objects were seen can still be missed (see the connector description for the full list of known limits). Cost: memory for the objects modified within the window (limit about 256 MiB; beyond it the window is shortened with a warning s3.source.dedupe_window_shrunk, which lowers the tolerance for late-visible objects, so lower this value instead), and redelivery (at-least-once) of the objects modified within the window after a restart and when the snapshot hands over to CDC. Listing cost does not depend on it. Values above 1h log a warning, above 24h are rejected, and 0 disables the lookback. |  |
| `pollingPeriod` | duration | 1s | no | polling period for the CDC mode, formatted as a time.Duration string. |  |
| `prefix` | string |  | no | the S3 key prefix. |  |
| `sdk.batch.delay` | duration | 0 | no | Maximum delay before an incomplete batch is read from the source. |  |
| `sdk.batch.size` | int | 0 | no | Maximum size of batch before it gets read from the source. | greater-than(-1) |
| `sdk.schema.context.enabled` | bool | true | no | Specifies whether to use a schema context name. If set to false, no schema context name will be used, and schemas will be saved with the subject name specified in the connector (not safe because of name conflicts). |  |
| `sdk.schema.context.name` | string |  | no | Schema context name to be used. Used as a prefix for all schema subject names. If empty, defaults to the connector ID. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.key.enabled` | bool | false | no | Whether to extract and encode the record key with a schema. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.key.subject` | string | key | no | The subject of the key schema. If the record metadata contains the field "opencdc.collection" it is prepended to the subject name and separated with a dot. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.payload.enabled` | bool | false | no | Whether to extract and encode the record payload with a schema. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.payload.subject` | string | payload | no | The subject of the payload schema. If the record metadata contains the field "opencdc.collection" it is prepended to the subject name and separated with a dot. |  |
| `sdk.schema.extract.type` | string | avro | no | The type of the payload schema. | inclusion(avro) |
